runs.analysis:
The stage includes a tweak: scope/length budget of 5-7 most critical areas with concise fields. Candidate A has 7 items, which complies. Candidate B has 14 items, which is double the upper limit and is the verbose failure mode the tweak was meant to prevent. B is also lengthy and repetitive.

Content: A is more specific and decision-useful. It names concrete tools (PLAXIS, OpenSees, MIKE 21), sets quantitative targets (±1% buoyancy, ±15% hydrodynamic forces), and states sensitivity-scored assumptions with reasoning. It flags that the 18-month ratification assumption is optimistic. It notes that 50+ passenger rescue submersibles exceed current capacity. It also raises decompression and thermal issues. A has some flaws: ISSMGE does not certify PSHA specialists, "CUMACOUS" and "Marine Bioacoustics Simulator" look invented, and the AREMA and EUARS references are dubious. The "Aalborg University's DHI" and "BMT ARGOSS" details are off. The summary recommends moving the mobilization date to 2030-31, which is a sensible realism check. A also says the rail 25kV vs 3kV DC mismatch is an electrification matter, which is correct. It has a few quirks, such as a 10 atm decompression issue and treating a 14 km corridor as an assumption.

B: it includes more areas (maritime traffic, financing, corrosion, climate, decommissioning, supply chain), which are legitimately relevant. However, it breaks the scope budget. It mostly restates the plan's mitigation claims as data to collect. Several errors: it labels signaling as "25kV AC vs 3kV DC", which is electrification, not signaling. It uses invented named people (Dr. Kenji Tanaka etc., possibly from team.md, so that may be fine). It uses "Engage Dr. Kenji Tanaka to validate borehole interpretations", which is an internal-validation conflict. It treats an "independent seismic review panel" as validating climate design. It lists "workforce planning SAP" simulation for offshore residential platforms at 100 m depth, which makes little sense. Its assumptions are mostly "High" and just restate plan claims, with less critical sensitivity scoring. It lists "Consult IEEE standards committee" and "IPCC working group", which are impractical. "Install AIS at 10 locations" is not data collection. The summary lists 14 areas but in a different order than the items.

A is better overall, mainly for following the budget, being more specific and correct, and being more critical.

B is better. The stage budget caps the list at 5-7 critical areas with concise fields. A has 14 items, double the cap and the failure mode the tweak is meant to prevent. A's Summary also lists them in a different order from the actual items. B has 7 well-filled items. It adds testable quantitative assumption thresholds (buoyancy within ±2 m, CFD within ±15%) and critical notes: the 18-month ratification timeline is optimistic, 6 months of prototype monitoring may be too short, and current rescue submersibles carry about 18-24 passengers, not 50+. Its Summary also flags the unrealistic ASAP schedule and recommends a 2030-31 mobilization with phase gates. B has weaknesses: it omits financial structuring, has a few dubious tool and organization names (CUMACOUS, EUARS), and a questionable decompression-chamber claim. A is broader but more repetitive, and some of its SMART dates are unrealistic (for example, the contingency reserve "by September 2026"). B fits the format and constraints better and is more useful downstream.

Candidate A has four concise items (RTE timeline, land holding costs, DGSI isolation, workforce). It omits tenant demand and financing, cooling/PUE and fiber, all of which are critical gates for a 9 GW red-team plan. Its Summary mislabels the workforce item as "Data Item 3" when it is item 4. Some of its assumptions are weak or optimistic. Candidate B has seven items covering every major gate. It is far more specific, with named RTE and DREAL engagement, a tenant-funnel and debt-covenant model, dated multi-step SMART objectives, and kill/pivot triggers. It is verbose and has errors: the holding-cost per-hectare figure is inconsistent with its stated annual total, sub-2 ms RTT to London is unrealistic, and a "<€X" placeholder is left in. Even so, it is much more useful for downstream planning.

Candidate A has 7 items, at the top of the 5–7 budget. It covers the critical validation areas: grid/RTE, land and buffers, DGSI/ANSSI, tenant demand and financing, cooling/PUE, fiber, and workforce. Each item has concrete data requests, named tools, expert validation steps, and multi-date SMART objectives that fit a May 2026 start. It ties items to the plan's strategic decisions and gates, and its notes include fallbacks and pivots. It has real flaws: a holding-cost arithmetic error (€50–75k/ha/year totalled as €6.4–9.6M, when 12,880 ha would cost about €640M+), a physically implausible sub-2 ms RTT assumption to London and Frankfurt, odd vendor and tool references, a leftover "<€X" placeholder, and some verbosity. Candidate B is concise but has only 4 items. It omits tenant demand and financing, cooling/water, and fiber, which are core feasibility gates. It has an "N/A" simulation step, thin one-line SMART objectives, and a summary that mislabels items (workforce is called item 3 but is item 4). It makes fewer blunders but gives much less decision-useful content for downstream stages. A's coverage and specificity outweigh its errors.

Candidate A is stronger. It has 7 items, which is at the top of the 5-7 budget. Each item is plan-specific and ties back to the strategic decisions, the expert review and the risks. It covers the main validation areas: clearing float and velocity, enforcement politics, PRM/accessibility timing, distributor economics of the 5% royalty, T+5 latency feasibility, governance agility, and contingency activation. Its data items are real data (latency measurements, fee benchmarks, bank guarantee quotes). Its simulation steps name tools and parameters. Its SMART objectives have dates and thresholds that fit the 2026-05 start. Weaknesses: the fields are long, so it ignores the "concise fields" tweak. A few numbers are shaky: the €50–150M monthly velocity looks low, the €50–200M per-operator capex overlaps with private IT spend, and the €90M "10%" figure is odd. It also under-covers demand and modal-shift data, and it is repetitive in places.

Candidate B is concise, but it has only 3 items. It misses important validation areas: market demand and modal shift versus air, distributor adoption, accessibility depth, and clearing velocity. Its "Data to Collect" entries are often deliverables or tasks, such as "Draft Technical Failure Criteria report" and "Sample audit templates", not data. Its simulation steps are thin (two per item). It is internally inconsistent: it assumes the strict tiered liability model is legally sound while its own notes recommend pivoting away from it. The SMART objective "within 160% of €300M" is odd, and the summary refers to "tasks detailed below" that never appear. It is less useful for downstream planning.

Overall, A's depth and specificity outweigh its verbosity, and B is too sparse and has weaker content.

Both candidates follow the expected structure and reference strategic decisions, experts, and the Builder scenario. The stage prompt says to apply a scope/length budget: 5-7 critical areas with concise fields.

Candidate A has 3 items. That is concise but below the 5-7 target. It covers liability, latency, and cost recovery. It omits major areas such as distributor adoption, governance, and the accessibility schema as its own item. The items are reasonably specific, but some are weak. One example is "Expert 6" being used for two different roles. Another is the SMART objective for Item 1, "within 160% of the €300M reserve", which is odd. The dates (2027-03) fit the start of the project. The Summary says "detailed below" but isn't a real summary. The overall content is thin.

Candidate B has 7 items, which is the top of the target range. They cover float adequacy, enforcement viability, accessibility, distributor adoption, T+5 latency, governance, and contingency protocols. Each item has detailed, plan-specific data, simulations, and validations, with SMART objectives and notes tied to the expert review. It is very long, and it ignores the "concise fields" budget, because each field has 4-5 long bullets. It has some flaws. Some assumptions are invented, such as 10% of capacity budget = €90M, and "capex €50–€200M per operator". The date 2026-06-14 for the TSC workshop is plausible given the 2026-05-14 start. Some SMART objectives are overloaded. Item 7 is somewhat process-heavy. Even so, it covers the plan's risks more completely and is more useful downstream. Its team names are consistent with team.md. A's dates in 2027 are not wrong, but B's earlier dates fit an ASAP start better.

B is better on faithfulness, specificity, coverage, and usefulness. The only advantage A has is conciseness, and A's item count is below the budget.

Candidate A delivers seven well-developed items. They cover vulnerable-population identification, alert thresholds and governance, cooling centers, home-intervention procurement, health data and triage, outreach staffing and safety, and gate metrics. Together these cover most of the plan's critical areas. Each item has concrete data to collect, simulation steps, expert validation, SMART objectives, and risks with contingencies. It names Leipzig and ties to the plan's gates and budget.

A has some weaknesses. Several SMART dates are unrealistic or inconsistent: the "M1.5" labels, the Month 2 gate at 2026-06-15, and a threshold finalization date of 2026-05-10. Some assumptions are oddly rated. For example, "Low" is given to an assumption that could be risky (emergency water supply). The home-intervention targets (5,000 kits at ≤€150 per unit, 40% of the budget) may be invented, and the arithmetic is inconsistent: 5,000 × €150 = €750k, not €1.4M. Mentions of "social media" and "IVR" slightly conflict with the plan's constraints. Even so, A is comprehensive and decision-useful. It covers the key regulatory, data-protection and market issues (procurement, suppliers).

Candidate B has only four items. It is more narrowly tied to internal pipeline artifacts, such as "Expert Review 2.6.C", "Decision 10" and "Missing" roles. That makes it read as meta-commentary and less self-contained. It omits thresholds, outreach/GDPR identification, worker protection, and communications. Its content is thin: 2 simulation steps and 2 assumptions per item. It does include a useful financial-governance item (the €300k contingency reserve). But it contains inconsistencies. For example, it says "€1.7M remaining after MCR" and treats an MCR carved out of the initial tranche as unusual. It also shifts to 1,000 units. It has few data-gathering actions (market quotes and similar). It also uses "(Missing)" role labels, which are odd.

Overall, A is clearly stronger on specificity, coverage, and usefulness. B is more concise but too narrow, and it is more dependent on prior artifacts.

Candidate A has four concise items (cooling centers, health data loop, home installation, financial reserve). It is tied to upstream pivots and has a useful finance item. But it is below the 5–7 area budget and omits threshold calibration, outreach feasibility, procurement and market data, and gate metric design. It also never names the city, lists experts as "(Missing)", and contradicts itself on installation budget share (100% vs 50%). Candidate B has seven items within the 5–7 budget. It covers nearly all plan scopes and both gates, names Leipzig and the DWD, and gives concrete data and simulation actions: temperature percentiles, supplier quotes, an inter-rater study, a safety dry run, and a mock gate audit. Its SMART objectives are dated and it includes contingencies. Its weaknesses are length, some inconsistent numbers (40% of €3.5M vs 5,000 units at €150), the assumption that housing associations will share data without MOUs, a "Jan–Dec" model for a May start, and a voucher fallback that contradicts the equity pivot. B is far more useful downstream and its flaws are smaller than A's coverage gaps.
